content.text:
Rob Field
CFO, RCL Foods
Slide 15 deals with our CapEx spends in the period and forecasted. We had previously signaled that we would see slightly higher forecasted spends, and those are slowly coming through, mostly related to catch-up spends in sugar and chicken. What you're seeing here is also some expansionary CapEx sitting within our baking business unit and Vector Logistics. A shift toward more expansion CapEx, but overall the same in terms of a working capital comment. The overall remains well managed when you judge the spend against a variety of metrics, whether they be percentage of free cash or percentage of revenue. They're still very acceptable references, and our ultimate test is the see-through in terms of how this translates to an underlying improving return on invested capital, which is on the next slide. Slide 16.
The put up of this at an interim is always a little bit challenging or more difficult to interpret by virtue of obviously it being a rolling twelve-month reference. What you're doing is you're picking up the H2 of previous financial years, and particularly evident when you look at Chicken and Vector's prior period reported ROIC numbers, which are very big negatives, largely because that goes back to the period where we booked some of the impairments. Overall, especially on an underlying basis, you see the improving trend, especially pleasing results coming through our food division. Vector is improving as well in line with the trajectory of the planned consolidation of their networks, post the Imperial Cold Logistics acquisition. There's still road to travel on that, but a pleasing improvement.
Chicken is quite fairly remains challenged. We are in the process of that turnaround. Marthinus will give us some color to that a little bit later. Then the last two slides, I've included in the deck, but I'm not gonna spend any time on them. It really is the how we find ourselves from a debt package perspective with our commitments and governance underlying, which are all in very good space. Really nothing to highlight other than just to record them here for your benefit. I'm now gonna hand back to Paul.
Paul Cruickshank
CEO, RCL Foods
Thanks, Rob. Just moving on to the food division results. Just a reminder that the landing page of each of the business units does reconcile the actual reported results of underlying performance, as Rob has highlighted. This is to give the market a clear view of the true performance of each of these business units. Food division, a reminder as well, comprises groceries, baking, and sugar. The statutory EBITDA growth, which is slightly down on the prior year, but 1.9% ahead on an underlying basis. Moving to slide 22, which is the groceries underlying EBITDA, is 2.4% on the up on the prior year, primarily driven by growth in grocery, despite price increases implemented to counter higher commodity costs.
Strong volume recovery in pies was built off a lower COVID base, and heightened cost focus and the consolidation of operations in beverages also contributed to improved grocery results. If we move to the next slide, with culinary categories within grocery, which has remained resilient despite the competitive trading environment and commodity input price pressure. Our Nola brand retained its market leadership position, and a new economy proposition was launched under the brand, which is gaining traction. Yum Yum's share growth is also pleasing, considering the volume of imported peanut butter in the market, which does not attract a tariff, whereas the raw peanut imports do. Albeit slow progress is still being made with ITAC in attempts to align the approach to peanut and peanut butter imports.
focus on the culinary categories of the upcoming year will be on delivering operating efficiencies and driving a pricing strategy that best mitigates the margin risk associated with the high input costs. If we move to the next slide, it is pet food. It highlights the strong performance in our category, despite the category being under pressure. This is reflected by growing market share positions across most brands. Furthermore, branded pet food volumes grew by 9.2%, offsetting the loss of lower margin BOP business. More specifically, our premium retail and veterinary ranges are well positioned, delivering strong growth, and our Optimizor brand performs continues to outperform in the co-op channel. A raft of exciting pet food innovation is ready to launch into the market once approved by the relevant government departments. Moving to slide 24.
Pieman's operating units has seen good recovery in volume on the back of strong promotional plan and growth coming in from innovation, the Pieman's Big Deal pie and the newly launched frozen Pieman's range in the retail channel. Margins have, however, come under pressure, primarily due to significant raw material cost increases. Saving initiatives aimed at mitigating margin risk and landing necessary price increases will be a key focus area. Our beverages business has delivered improved performance from a cost perspective, with the consolidation of the Ultra-high Temperature and Fresh yielding the anticipated efficiency benefits. However, volume growth remains muted as the category struggles to recover post the COVID lockdown, with significant distributors' service level challenges compounding this in the most recent months. Moving to slide 25.
Although our bread, buns, and rolls operating units have seen strong volume growth during the period, particularly on bread, underlying EBITDA across the baking business is down on the prior. Margins have been challenged as price increases landed have only partially offset wheat cost pressure. External milling volumes have been under increasing pressure as the business focused on protecting margins amidst the rising wheat price. On slide 26, the bread, buns, and rolls operating units achieved good volume growth, largely on the back of the new depot rollout program, which is part of the bigger Sunbake growth strategy. Performance for the period was especially pleasing considering price increases necessitated by high raw material and diesel costs. The capital expansion project at Polokwane bakery is on track and will be commissioned before the end of the financial year. Moving to slide 27.
An improved operational performance drove the milling result, supported by the early benefits of the ERP planning system that is being implemented at our Pretoria site. The launch of a new coating product for the QSR market also contributed to the improved result. The specialty operating unit delivered a disappointing result with margins under pressure due to increased input costs and a shift in mix. Therefore, improved efficiency throughout the plant consolidation initiative will be a key strategic focus area for the business over the next two years. Moving to slide 28. Sugar produced a strong result aided by continued focus on our controllables, coupled with higher international sugar prices and favorable local industry factors. Slide 29 unpacks Sugar's results in more detail, which is underpinned by increased local demand, together with a 42% increase in the international sugar price, which improved export earnings for the period.
The continued focus on cost control across the value chain also contributed to the strong result. On the downside, cane quality and yields were temporarily affected by an aphid infestation and heat in the early part of the season. The fire that Rob mentioned at Komati sugar warehouse in October destroyed 40,000 tons of sugar and disrupted operations in the last quarter. The insurance process is progressing well, and the business has appointed a team to design the optimal future storage solution for sugar. On slide 50, Molatek delivered a strong performance for the period, especially considering the prior period's exceptional result, which was bolstered by farmers rebuilding their herds post the drought. Higher raw material prices are starting to put pressure on margins, and as a result, the business is focused on managing costs and driving an improved mix to mitigate this as much as possible.
I'll now hand over to Marthinus.
Marthinus Stander
CEO, Rainbow Chicken
morning and thank you, Paul. Right, moving to the first slide. I think the key here is the low base. If one looks at EBITDA performance, we're still talking relatively very small numbers. However, there was an improvement. I think what bodes well for us is that the revenue was increased as a result of making more products, selling more, and on the back of better prices in the market. We had a very challenging start to the financial year in the first two months, mainly as a result of avian influenza and also obviously the looting incident. Moving to the next slide. I think we've laid down some significant building blocks in supporting our business and particularly the turnaround. It'll stand us in good stead.
Specific reference to the regional management model, the centralized model, integrating the value chain elements within these three regions: feed, breed, agric processing, distribution, and sales. Creating that focus that one requires, giving us the focus particularly on the agric side of things. We are in essence an agric business. So your KPIs and the number of chicks that you can produce, the number of eggs, on the back of your hatchability and your livability is obviously key to lower cost. We have introduced the new breed. It is a process that needs to roll out and one will only see that benefit really during calendar year 2023. It will be more significant in F24, as this process rolls out.
We see a significant reduction in imports, mostly driven by the avian influenza in Europe. I think AI is very much a very volatile space at the moment. The industry has embarked on programs to do proper surveillance. We see it's still circulating in our birds, and there's lots of AI in Europe. One also looks towards contingency measures to be more prepared should one again have a very intense period during the next winter. Moving to the final slide. Here we refer to specifically the external feed business of Epol. It is a time, as Paul also mentioned, where one tries to protect margin in the absence of just growing new business, which one will have to discount given the current state of affairs in a prolonged bullish commodity market.
One's best defense here is to try and add value to your customer's business and to focus on cost reduction. Thank you very much. That's from my side, and I think I hand over to Chris.
Chris Esterhuizen
Operations Manager, RCL Foods
Thanks, Marthinus, and good morning, everybody. Moving to slide 36
Just looking at the headlines, we see pleasing revenue growth to just over ZAR 1.8 billion, driven predominantly by the recovery in our food service volumes to almost pre-COVID levels. Good growth in retail and our LNA Zambia business consolidation, for the first time, offset partially by the unrest in July. The next bullet under headlines, I'll talk to in the next slide, which is the good progress we've made on the final phase of the Imperial Cold Logistics network. Just commenting on our EBITDA, you can see a growth of nearly 12% and our underlying adjusted basis, with the impact of COVID equating to about 9.2%, but pleasing nonetheless and on track with our turnaround. Turning to the next slide.
We've spoken about the revenue growth, just focusing in on the final phase three of our network integration, and pleased to say that our capacity builds are complete in some of the areas, namely Port Elizabeth late last year. Bloemfontein, we're just coming online with that capacity build now, expansion build. Durban and Polokwane due over the coming months. By the end of the financial year, by June, we will have the integration complete. There has been some delays due to international supply chain challenges and COVID primarily. The good news is that is coming to finality.
Down the bottom of the page on the right-hand side, you can see our final end state of 7 sites and approximately 350 vehicles from where, the far left you had 14 sites and 445 vehicles. It gives you a bit of a feel of the integration benefits that we'll get once done. Moving to the final slide, and really a quite exciting area for us, our EmptyTrips, which is a digital freight matching platform. As I've said previously, we've rolled out internally, and we're in the process now of rolling this out to the external market. We're excited by this opportunity, and we'll watch this space as we go into the external marketplace. With that, thanks. Paul, I hand back to you.
Paul Cruickshank
CEO, RCL Foods
Thanks, Chris. Just moving to the prospect slide, and I'll just summarize. The key themes have already been mentioned, but GDP growth in South Africa is expected to be less than 2% over the next few years. There's no doubt that the economic conditions will remain tough for the foreseeable future, and that along with higher inflation will place more pressure on the consumers. We are acutely aware of this. The current situation in Ukraine will contribute to a further rise in commodity costs, the extensive impact of which is currently unknown. Just summing up quickly the outlook for the next six months. We expect to continue the resilient performance from Groceries.
Sugar will continue to focus on its operational efficiency as the season starts up, though the full year results will not be at the record levels in the last fiscal year, and are expected to be materially lower due to previously mentioned agricultural challenges. However, despite this, we still expect to see the second-highest profit in the business unit's history. While Chicken has made strides, as Marthinus indicated in implementing its turnaround strategy, it is not yet at the right level of profitability, mainly due to the breed challenges which he explained in more detail. Vector's also made good progress with its turnaround and is well on track to deliver further once its capacity builds are complete. We will continue to drive the managed separation of Chicken and Vector as a priority in a well-considered manner. That wraps up the formal part of the presentation.
Thank you for your attendance, and I look forward to hearing from you. Over to you, Darren.
[Company Representative] (RCL Foods)
Company Representative, RCL Foods
Thanks, Paul. We are now starting the Q&A portion of our webcast. A reminder of the two ways the questions can be asked. First, please kindly submit your questions on the Q&A tab, or if you would like to ask a question live, kindly raise your virtual hand. Your name will be called out before we unmute you. Please state your company name, who the question is directed to, followed by your question. We have already received some questions in our Q&A tab, which I'll kick us off on. The first one pertains to chicken. The comment reads, "Congrats to Marthinus and his team in dragging Rainbow back into profit in very difficult circumstances with AI, soaring input costs and genetic issues. Can I ask for opinions please on, one, timeframe to get genetics back to normal?
2, do you believe the current consumer will take any more price increases in 2022? 3, due to global and local issues, maize, soya are elevated. Can I get your view on the H2 input cost scenario as at these levels? What is Rainbow's view on input costs and how it's positioned itself? Thanks. Marthinus, if I can pass over to you.
Marthinus Stander
CEO, Rainbow Chicken
Thanks, Darren, and hi Anthony, and thank you for your good wishes. Yeah, I think I did speak about the timeframe. First placements on GP side is taking place and then, Anthony, as you would know, there's quite a time lapse, going from grandparent to parent to broiler every month. Every time about a 7-month gap. Significant contribution will come, in the 2023 calendar year, more towards the middle of it that year, leading to F24, as that progeny, you know, process rolls out.
In terms of the commodity markets, I think I also expressed a view that we see that the fundamentals point to, you know, and particularly on the maize side are pretty good stocks-to-usage ratios. Fundamentals have not played out. More technical matters, funds with long positions. In this current scenario of high volatility and adding to the mix the Ukrainian prices, it's hard to see that the commodity, you know, the prices are just gonna come back. I think we're in for a bit more of a high jump. It links to obviously our capability or capacity to pass on price.
I think we're in for a high food inflation period, but whether the consumer can manage that is the big question, and it is obviously a big and a huge risk factor in our lives. It's hard to say. Price has to move given the input cost and we'll obviously do our best. Thank you.
[Company Representative] (RCL Foods)
Company Representative, RCL Foods
Thanks, Marthinus. The next question relates to Vector. A comment is Vector has a good performance. Is the business actually still a core holding of RCL Foods, as there has been informed whispers in some logistics channels that Vector's on the block with some rivals celebrating its opportunity to acquire it. Does RCL actually plan to further clean up its disparate structure to create value? I'll hand over to Paul.
Paul Cruickshank
CEO, RCL Foods
Thanks, Darren. Thanks, Anthony, for the question. Slide five is really where we set out the strategic intent, which is not similar to what we said at September full year results announcement. Vector, Chicken, and Sugar over a period of time, as and when appropriate, we will find the right option for them. We don't know what that option is yet, and we'll evaluate each one on its merits as and when those options arise. What we have done now is focused on what I call the administrative part of it. We have done that, and when we will consider how we take it forward. As I did say, we will update the market as it's been appropriate on any one of those business unit divisions and how we plan to proceed with them.
[Company Representative] (RCL Foods)
Company Representative, RCL Foods
Thanks, Paul. The next query reads: You mentioned that you are firm on which categories you would like to expand into organically and inorganically. Which categories are these?
Paul Cruickshank
CEO, RCL Foods
I'm happy to take that one. Thanks, Darren. Yeah, we've done a lot of work on our category, assessing category landscape. Obviously, what I'm not gonna share is what those categories are. We're not gonna show our hand to our competitors. What we clear on is where our brands can extend to, in what we call adjacent categories, and that would be organic growth. That one we are clear on, and we'll really begin that process. The inorganic and the acquisition type activity will be very focused, again, underpinned by those categories we wanna play in. What I'll just share is the criteria needs to be that they're branded, that it is growing from a market perspective, and that it is margin accretive to our RCL Foods' portfolio.
[Company Representative] (RCL Foods)
Company Representative, RCL Foods
Thank you. The next query is quite similar, relates to slide 5 of our presentation, where Sugar is grouped in with other FMCG value-added products and said that the operating model will remain unchanged in the medium term. Does this mean that Sugar will remain in the portfolio for the foreseeable future? If that's correct, then why was this unit separated into a separate legal entity?
Paul Cruickshank
CEO, RCL Foods
Darren, thanks. Happy to just pick that up, and I've answered most of it earlier. I'll just pick up the specific pieces. Let me start with the second part, is that Sugar was always a separate legal entity, and there was actually no work to do there. There was more work around Chicken separation, and Vector was also a separate legal entity. Chicken had been integrated into the old consumer division. That answers why we separated it. And for all three of them, what it was is preparing ourselves for what the future may be. The second one around Sugar, I earlier described that we'll do it on a basis that makes sense for each one of those businesses.
All we're saying is that from an operational perspective, currently Sugar will remain as part of the food division, and there's no change in the way in which we are operationally running that business, and we'll assess that as we go along.
[Company Representative] (RCL Foods)
Company Representative, RCL Foods
Great. Thank you, Paul. The next query reads: How far forward is RCL hedged from a wheat perspective?
Paul Cruickshank
CEO, RCL Foods
We obviously don't share our positions to the market. I think what is important is just to acknowledge that we do import wheat from the Ukraine. The impact of that will need to be assessed. It was only last week's news, so we're busy doing that. In the lead up to what has transpired in the last week, we did extend our physicals, because that obviously is a key focus point now as opposed to your actual hedge position. We have to have physicals to enable us to make bread. Our emphasis has shifted to mitigating that risk. Suffice to say that, given the circumstances, we are quite short, and have been short across all our commodities, for quite an extended period of time.
[Company Representative] (RCL Foods)
Company Representative, RCL Foods
Thank you, Paul. A query related to sugar tax. The Minister of Finance increased sugar tax from ZAR 0.021 per gram to ZAR 0.023. Suffice to say this looks negligible. Can you please put into context for us and perhaps comment on what the potential impact could be?
Paul Cruickshank
CEO, RCL Foods
To be honest, this was a surprise to us last week. We are busy working with industry to assess what the impact is. The extent of the reformulation, at this point, is unknown. What is the concern is government's indication that they will target other soft drinks, as opposed to carbonated, which was in the first round of the sugar tax. We will work with industry and government to understand this. It was a surprise in a sense that the master plan clearly said that the sugar tax would not be extended beyond existing categories, that has been increased and an indication to extend. We need to assess the impact of this and understand from government what this actually means, and also to our customers what they intend to do from a formulation perspective.
[Company Representative] (RCL Foods)
Company Representative, RCL Foods
Thank you, Paul. As a related query in terms of some new news is for your logistics business, can you give us an indication of the impact of record high fuel prices?
Chris Esterhuizen
Operations Manager, RCL Foods
On the fuel, thanks, Darren. We do a fuel neutrality, so we recover, in most instances, the impact of fuel. It's in our contracts, and we keep on a fuel neutral basis.
[Company Representative] (RCL Foods)
Company Representative, RCL Foods
Thank you, Chris. The following query is: What was the rationale behind including waste value operations as part of the chicken division? This is likely to make it difficult for investors to get a sense of any turnaround initiatives in the chicken business. I'm gonna pass this over to Rob Field.
Rob Field
CFO, RCL Foods
Thanks, Darren. It really goes with the theme of what Paul referenced earlier in terms of tidying up the housekeeping within the business, readying the different parts for whatever might be a destination for them. Obviously, the waste value plants are an integral part of both the Worcester and Rustenburg operations, and so belongs in that space. At this juncture, it is not a material contributor, and so certainly wouldn't distort or give you an inability to understand the turnaround within the chicken business. That we'll certainly make clear into the future. No issues there.
[Company Representative] (RCL Foods)
Company Representative, RCL Foods
Thank you very much, Rob. I see we've got a hand up by Chris Logan. Chris, we are going to unmute you. Please will you then state where you are from, your question, and who you would like your question directed to.
Chris Logan
Owner and CIO, Opportune Investments
Hello. Hi. Yes, it's Chris Logan, Opportune Investments. Can you hear me?
[Company Representative] (RCL Foods)
Company Representative, RCL Foods
Yes. Thank you, Chris.
Chris Logan
Owner and CIO, Opportune Investments
Yes. Hi. Well, congrats on all the progress. Just looking at things from a historical perspective and with what's known about your strategic review, it seems that your strategic review has set you on the course to attain shareholder value through focus or what you call a pure play environment, which is all very well and good, and I'm sure there's a lot of wisdom in that. But if you look back at the group, the problem's been the absence of returns. For instance, I think you've got to go back to 2011 to find a year in which ROE was greater than 10%, and your ROIC's been below 10% since you started measuring it. You know, you do get groups who are unfocused and generate higher returns and hence share all the value.
I mean, Associated British Foods would be one. Perhaps you could just clarify how you see focus is gonna lead to higher returns or, you know, if you take my point that ultimately it's generating higher returns that generates value.
Paul Cruickshank
CEO, RCL Foods
I'm happy to answer that. Rob, if you feel like you're welcome to chip in. Thanks, Chris. Yes, what we announced in August, September was the over the period of the managed separation, what chicken and sugar, let me start with those two, brings volatility to the environment, given the agricultural nature of those businesses. That's what we long term are seeking to steer away from. Vector is a different conversation. Vector, to a large extent, now has all of the frozen basket in South Africa, and our internal terminology is that it's largely outgrown RCL Foods and where we wanna focus on going forward. I hear you. Other businesses have different models. I hear you about returns.
Hence the volatility of chicken and sugar is what needs to be considered. The third piece is the focus on brands, and that's where you get a more sustainable earnings and more sustainable cash flow. That's ultimately what we're looking for.
[Company Representative] (RCL Foods)
Company Representative, RCL Foods
Thank you, Paul. Moving over to a query for Vector. There seems to have been good results from Vector. Is this due to base effects? Is there a better macro environment for logistics in South Africa? Question for Chris.
Chris Esterhuizen
Operations Manager, RCL Foods
Thank you. Yes. I think as we said in the presentation, there is some base effects in that we are still integrating the two supply chain networks, and that's coming to an end in the next few months. We have some base effects there. We've had the benefit of our food service business coming up to almost pre-COVID volumes. Those are the two big drivers.
[Company Representative] (RCL Foods)
Company Representative, RCL Foods
Thank you very much, Chris. Another comment and query has come through saying there has been sector talk that PepsiCo has asked Pioneer Foods to exit certain private label type of products, and that has seen competitors, I'm told, pick up nice manufacturing contracts. Has RCL picked up some of these contracts or wish to participate? Handing over to Paul.
Paul Cruickshank
CEO, RCL Foods
Yeah, thanks, Darren. The answer is we haven't picked up any contracts. What we do is we participate in either manufacturing contracts or dealer-owned brands where it makes commercial sense for us, and over a period have won and lost in this area. We're open for business in this area, but it will depend on the commercial terms of those contracts.
[Company Representative] (RCL Foods)
Company Representative, RCL Foods
Thanks very much, Paul. A question for Rob. Will RCL look at some form of refinancing of its debt at the end of its current five-year debt package?
Rob Field
CFO, RCL Foods
We certainly will, mostly because we are obliged to. I think where we find ourselves now is a very comfortable position to be able to restructure at a lower level of package than what we've historically had. Obviously, the clear juncture we find ourselves at in terms of the strategic repositioning of the business needs to be considered at the same time. We have 18 months to run on the package, so we've got time on our hands. There are some repayment obligations, which I mentioned in the presentation. Plenty of time to be able to reposition ourselves in this space.
Yes, very comfortable that a destination we would include some level of debt in our overall capital structure.
[Company Representative] (RCL Foods)
Company Representative, RCL Foods
Thank you, Rob. The next query is, given that Polokwane bakery is on track for commissioning before financial year-end, how do you plan to make sure that you get to the right operating capacity sooner? And what is the view on competitor activity in the baking division?
Paul Cruickshank
CEO, RCL Foods
With regards to the first one, you obviously have a summer-winter peak in bread. We're currently transitioning in the next couple of months towards the more demand-driven winter period. Hence, the capacity will come on stream hopefully prior to that demand peaking from July onwards. We have restarted in terms of growth from existing bakery capacity in the summer period, so rolling out our depots, et cetera, that I spoke about earlier in advance of that capacity coming on stream. Competitor activity in the baking division. Obviously, the market is pretty fierce in the retail sector. Just a reminder that our mix between general trade and retail is much higher than the majority of our competitors, so we're more focused in the general trade area.
Yes, the retail promotional activity is pretty fierce right now in bread, and is likely to continue with the wheat prices as they currently stand.
[Company Representative] (RCL Foods)
Company Representative, RCL Foods
Thank you, Paul. At this point, we have no further questions on either the Q&A chat or on our live option. Paul, if you'd like to close off.
Paul Cruickshank
CEO, RCL Foods
Yeah. Thank you very much, everybody for your participation and for your questions. We appreciate it, and we look forward to chatting again at year-end.
[Company Representative] (RCL Foods)
Company Representative, RCL Foods
Thank you, Paul. Ladies and gentlemen, that concludes our webcast. Thank you for joining us. You may now disconnect.

Operator
Good morning. My name is Shelby, and I'll be your conference operator today. At this time, I would like to welcome everyone to Royal Caribbean Group's Business Update and Fourth Quarter 2021 Earnings Call. All participants are in a listen-only mode. After the speaker presentation, there will be a question and answer session. To ask a question during the session, you'll need to press star one on your telephone. I would now like to introduce Michael McCarthy, Vice President of Investor Relations. Mr. McCarthy, the floor is yours.
Michael McCarthy
VP of Investor Relations, Royal Caribbean Group
Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today for our Business Update and Fourth Quarter and Full Year 2021 Financial Results Earnings Call. Joining me here in Miami are Jason Liberty, our Chief Executive Officer, Naftali Holtz, our Chief Financial Officer, and Michael Bayley, President and CEO of Royal Caribbean International. Before we get started, I'd like to note that we will be making forward-looking statements during this call. These statements are based on management's current expectations and are subject to risks and uncertainties. A number of factors could cause actual results to differ materially from our current expectations. Please refer to our earnings release issued this morning, as well as our filings with the SEC for a description of these factors. We do not undertake to update any forward-looking statements as circumstances change.
Also, we will be discussing certain non-GAAP financial measures, which are adjusted as defined, and a reconciliation of all non-GAAP items can be found on our website and in our earnings release available at www.rclinvestor.com. Jason will begin the call by providing a strategic overview and update on the business. Naftali will follow up with a recap of our fourth quarter and full year results, an update on our latest actions, and on the current booking environment. We will then open the call for your questions. With that, I'm pleased to turn the call over to Jason.
Jason Liberty
CEO, Royal Caribbean Group
Thank you, Michael, and good morning, everyone. I'm pleased to be with all of you today in my new role here at Royal Caribbean Group. I'm very fortunate and humbled to take the helm of this incredible organization, which includes our industry-leading brands and the most innovative fleet in the world that is enabled by our incredible people and culture. I'm very much looking forward to building on the company's remarkable legacy and track record in the years ahead. I also want to congratulate and welcome Naftali as our new CFO. Many of you already know Naf, but for those who don't, I'm confident you'll enjoy working with him.
Our mission at Royal Caribbean has been and continues to be focused simply and completely on delivering every day the very best vacation experience and doing so in a responsible way. It is awe-inspiring to see our team deliver on our mission each and every day. While 2021 was another challenging year for our company and the industry, it also marked our healthy return to sailing. In just a few short months, and thanks to the incredible preparedness of our operating team and crew throughout the last year and a half, we have brought back more than 85% of our capacity into service and delivered extraordinary vacations and memories to approximately 1.3 million guests.
I want to thank the hardworking people of the Royal Caribbean Group, both our crew and our shoreside employees, for their incredible efforts to bring back our fleet in such a short window and such a successful way. I am so proud and grateful for their efforts. I also want to thank our guests, travel partners, destination partners, suppliers, investors, and financial partners for their steadfast support. As we navigate through this Black Swan event, we have focused intently on a successful, healthy return to service, as you would expect.
At the same time, we have been charting our course to get back to pre-COVID performance levels and beyond soonest. The combination of very strong secular and demographic trends, our leading brands, the most innovative and a growing fleet, our global sourcing footprint, a leading technology platform, and the reshaping of our cost structure positions us exceptionally well to accelerate. Let me focus a moment on our healthy return to service.
Since we resumed operations, our goal has been to make cruising one of the safest vacations anywhere in the world while providing an exceptional guest experience. We continue to demonstrate that in a very tangible way. As you heard me say, we have carried approximately 1.3 million guests since the restart, with about 2,500 guests testing positive for COVID-19, a positivity rate of 0.19%. This positivity rate is still a small fraction of what it is in society at large, and nearly all cases on board were asymptomatic or had mild symptoms. Our rigorous health and safety protocols, with a 100% vaccination rate among our crew and close to a 100% vaccination rate among our guests, provide a safe environment where we can fulfill our mission of delivering amazing vacations. Our guests are responding by providing record Net Promoter Scores for us exceeding their expectations.
A few weeks ago, the prescriptive CDC Conditional Sailing Order expired, demonstrating the agency's confidence in the overall effectiveness of the health and safety protocols of the cruise industry. Our own protocols continue to go above and beyond anything the framework provided, and what consumers will find in any hospitality setting. We continue to engage with the CDC and other public health agencies as we look to adjust our COVID-19 risk mitigation measures in response to the changing nature of the virus. Our healthy return to service plans anticipated twists and turns on our recovery path. We remain nimble in our approach, adjusting to changes in the operating environment with a constant focus on our long-term strategy and success.
As everyone is aware, the Omicron variant has impacted most parts of society, as well as our operations. Since mid-December, we experienced an increase in the number of people testing positive for COVID on board our ships. The good news is that in the last several weeks, cases on board our ships have been declining rapidly, and we now have returned to exceptionally low pre-Omicron levels. In fact, over the last seven days, we have averaged only a handful of positive guest cases per cruise. With the declining cases, operational challenges are also abating. So while the variant is not done, it appears that the worst is behind us.
The timing of Omicron was particularly painful as the typical wave booking period begins in early January. So we do expect it will weigh on our performance in Q1 and, to a lesser extent, in early Q2. With the peak in Omicron now seemingly behind us, we have seen meaningful and sequential improvement in the booking activity week over week since the beginning of the year. In fact, in the last week of January, bookings returned to pre-Omicron levels, and we expect demand recovery to accelerate as the variant subsides. With that in mind, we have extended our sales and marketing activities for a delayed and extended wave.
While Omicron created some short-term challenges and will likely delay our return to profitability by a few months, our recovery trajectory remains intact. We remain confident that we will have a strong spring and summer season with great demand for cruising, both domestically and internationally. The robust secular trends of experiences over things that have propelled our business in the past few years are now recovering towards pre-COVID levels. We have also seen a change in the mindset of consumers coming out of the pandemic, with the desire to travel and re-engage with the world being stronger than ever.
In fact, the U.S. Travel Association research confirms that leisure travel will continue to increase at higher levels than business travel. All of this, coupled with consumer resilience and easing travel restrictions, provides tailwinds for our recovery. After a storied 2020 and 2021, we are eager to move forward in this new year. As people are keen on taking a vacation, we are ready to make their vacation dreams come true in a healthy and safe environment. We expect 2022 will be a strong transitional year as we bring the rest of our fleet into operations and approach historical occupancy levels. We expect a net loss for the first half of 2022 due to the impact of Omicron and a return to profitability in the second half of the year.
During 2022, we look forward to welcoming two additional new ships: Wonder of the Seas for Royal Caribbean International and Celebrity Beyond for Celebrity Cruises. These exciting new ships will deliver amazing vacations to our guests and join six other new vessels that have entered our fleet since 2020. This is a key pillar to support our recovery. New hardware is an important driver of quality demand, extraordinary customer experience, and exceptional financial performance. And just as important, it improves our sustainability as these are innovative ships that are much more energy efficient. We remain focused on continuing to innovate our product and maintain our strong competitive advantage, setting the foundation for a strong recovery and long-term profitable growth.
During the pandemic, we have had a relentless focus on reshaping our cost structure and rigorous capital allocation framework. We expect that the combination of new ships, growing yields, and higher profitability will propel our financial performance and support our focus to return to pre-COVID financial metrics and beyond soonest. Corporate stewardship remains another key priority as we continue to progress across environmental, social, and governance-focused areas. Climate change and reducing our emissions have been central to our environmental stewardship activities for decades.
Last quarter, we announced our comprehensive decarbonization strategy and goals. We realized that the transition to net zero will not be easy, and to achieve our ambitions, we will rely on our culture of innovation, as well as strong partnerships with governments, suppliers, and shipyards to develop alternative and accessible fuels and technologies. Additionally, in the past few months, we were named an employer of choice by Forbes and Glassdoor. Last week, we earned a 100% score on the Human Rights Campaign Foundation Corporate Equality Index, which rates corporate policies and practices that relate to LGBTQ+ workplace equality. These are recognitions we're proud of, and they reflect our commitment to our employees.
All of this tells you that our business model is incredibly strong, and we have a track record of growing revenue, earnings, and cash flow. Our formula for success is unchanged: recover and grow yields, enhance our margins, profitability, and ROIC. To that, we added returning our balance sheet to pre-COVID levels. We have the best brands in each of our segments, the most innovative fleet in the industry, exclusive destination experiences like Perfect Day at CocoCay, a nimble and effective global sourcing footprint, a leading technology platform, and most of all, the very best team both at sea and on land. With that winning formula, I am confident about the recovery, and I'm very excited about the future of Royal Caribbean Group. With that, I will turn it over to Naftali. Naf?
Naftali Holtz
CFO, Royal Caribbean Group
Thank you, Jason. Before I begin my remarks, I would like to share how energized I am to take on the Chief Financial Officer role. I will focus my energy on continuing the accelerated recovery and returning our performance metrics to pre-COVID levels as soon as possible while positioning the company for long-term success. I will now turn to discuss our results for the fourth quarter and full year 2021. This morning, we reported an adjusted net loss of $1.2 billion for the fourth quarter and $4.8 billion for the full year. It is important to note the Q4 results were better than our internal expectations, mainly due to continued strong onboard revenue performance and better cost management.
The financial results for 2021 reflect the impact on the suspension of sailing in the first half of the year and the tremendous effort to resume cruise operations and accelerate the flywheel in the second half. In the fourth quarter, we continued our return, bringing 12 more ships back into operations, building the load factors, and restarting our sales and marketing efforts, all to position the company for a successful 2022. Load factors for the quarter were 65% on core itineraries, with month-over-month improvements. We are incredibly pleased with the progress we have made in the fourth quarter. Our total load factors grew from 36% in Q3 to close to 60% in Q4. In addition, the continued strong onboard revenue contributed to a 10% increase in total gross revenue per passenger cruise day compared to the fourth quarter of 2019.
Cash flow from our operating ships turned positive in the fourth quarter. Now, I would like to discuss capacity and load factor expectations over the coming period. The Omicron variant caused short-term disruptions to the travel industry as well as our operations. As Jason just mentioned, our focus since we restarted operations has been to ensure the health and safety of our guests and crew, matching or exceeding guests' vacation experience expectations, and bringing the fleet up in a financially prudent way. With that in mind, we made the decision to cancel several sailings in the first quarter. We plan to operate about 7.7 million APCDs in Q1, or approximately 95% of our planned capacity. We expect that operating ships in the first quarter will be cash flow positive. Our capacity will further increase at the end of the quarter following the delivery of the incredible Wonder of the Seas.
Wonder will be introduced to the US market in March before heading to the Mediterranean for the summer season. Due to the impact from Omicron on near-term bookings and cancellations, we expect load factors of approximately 60% on core itineraries in Q1, with month-over-month improvement within the quarter. We also expect to bring the rest of our fleet back to service in time for the lucrative summer season. We expect our load factors to continue to steadily increase month-over-month and approach historical levels in the third quarter. While we offer cruises in the vast majority of our key destinations, we continue to closely monitor both China and Australia. We anticipate Australia to open for cruising for its summer season our winter time. With respect to China, it remains closed for cruising, and we have redeployed the remaining two ships planned in 2022 to other key markets.
We remain optimistic that we can capture long-term growth opportunities in the China market. Shifting to our balance sheet, we ended the year with $3.5 billion in liquidity, excluding the $1 billion issuance we completed in early January. We have ample liquidity to allow us to continue our recovery trajectory. During 2021, we focused on managing and improving our balance sheet. We reestablished access to the unsecured debt markets and successfully refinanced $2.3 billion of secured or guaranteed high-coupon debt. Our plan is to continue with these balance sheet improvement efforts throughout 2022. In early January, we issued $1 billion at 5.38% coupon, and we plan to use the proceeds to refinance near-term debt. In addition, we have taken and continue to take numerous actions to reshape our cost structure with a focus on further improving our leading pre-COVID margins.
While these actions will improve our cost structure and margin profile, we do anticipate that inflationary pressures and some transitory costs related to our healthy return to service will weigh on this year's earnings. Now, I'll provide an update on the demand environment and our 2022 sailings. For the last several quarters, we have seen new bookings improve from one quarter to the next. Bookings in the fourth quarter continued this positive trajectory, culminating in our biggest ever Black Friday and Cyber Weekend from the US. Bookings in the fourth quarter were up more than 75% compared to the third quarter. As we restarted our brand marketing programs in Q4, we generated strong demand to support the book of business for 2022 and 2023.
As the Omicron variant began spreading in December, we experienced slower booking activity and higher near-term cancellations over the holiday period, as many guests were testing positive before their cruise. But from the beginning of the year, we have seen meaningful week-over-week improvement in booking activity for both the first and the second half of 2022. Second-half booking activity has been recovering at a faster pace. In addition to that, we have seen a rapid improvement in cancellations over the same period. Similar to our experience with the Delta variant, as Omicron cases are beginning to decline, booking activity has begun to pick up. In fact, in the last week of January, bookings have returned to pre-Omicron levels. The UK, which is further ahead on the Omicron curve, has been on that improving trajectory for several weeks.
